About: Inner Product Invariance Under Coordinate Rotation

Source

Lecture
Lecture 2 — Vectors (Euclidean space, metric, inner product, the velocity vector).
Simulation
Simulation 1 — lecture visual aid: vectors A and B shown in two panels whose axes differ by a rotation θ; each panel shows the components and the inner product A·B; a slider sets θ; tips are draggable.
Concept
The inner product of two vectors — and therefore each vector's norm — is invariant under rotation of the coordinate axes, even though the individual components change.
Serves
Euclidean space as a geometric structure equipped with a metric; the Kronecker delta δij as the Cartesian metric; computing inner products and norms; the velocity vector as a coordinate-independent geometric object.
Inquiry
Rotate the frame — which of these changes: the components Ax, Ay; the length |A|; or the inner product A·B? Commit a prediction before running.
Misconception
That rotating the coordinate axes changes the inner product or a vector's length (confusing component change with geometric change).

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two frames, one plane

Let’s get our bearings. Both panels show the same plane; the S′ axes are simply turned counter-clockwise from the S axes by an angle θ. Nothing drawn in the plane is ever moved between the panels — only the axes it’s measured against. Each panel reports the coordinates of the point P, and later on the components, the lengths and the inner product u·V of two arrows.

2 · Predict — the length of V

Here’s your first prediction. The arrow V is drawn just once, and each panel reads its two components against its own axes — so those two pairs of numbers differ. What do you think happens to ‖V‖?

3 · Predict — the inner product

Now a second arrow, u, joins the first. Each panel forms u·V = uxVx + uyVy from its own components, and every one of those components differs between the panels. What do you think — the two results are…

4 · Predict — when u·V is zero

Try a special case. Suppose u is dragged until the boxed u·V reads 0.00 in Frame S. What do you think Frame S′ would show then?

Now go ahead and do it: drag the tip of u until u·V reads 0.00, and compare the two panels.

5 · Invariants

So let’s give this a name. A number that every rotated frame agrees on is called an invariant: ‖V‖, ‖u‖ and u·V are invariants, while the separate components aren’t. If V is a velocity, the components depend on how you lay down your axes, but ‖V‖ — the speed — doesn’t. Press ▶ Play to sweep θ and compare the two kinds of row.

Notation

▾
  • P — a point; its coordinates (x, y) in S differ from (x′, y′) in S′ when θ ≠ 0 or the S′ origin is translated.
  • Vx — x-component of V in Frame S; Vx′ — x′-component in Frame S′. Components depend on the frame; ‖V‖ does not.
  • θ — rotation angle of the S′ axes relative to S (counter-clockwise positive). t = (tx, ty) — translation of the S′ origin in S.
  • — Kronecker delta (Cartesian metric). ‖V‖ = ; u·V is invariant under rotation and translation.

Formal tools

Inner product via the Cartesian metric
Kronecker delta — the metric δij
Passive rotation of components (axes turn by +θ)
Norm (length) from the inner product
Why it is invariant — the cross terms cancel exactly

The inner product is the contraction of the components with the metric δij. In Cartesian coordinates δij is the same in every rotated frame, so although the components transform, the scalar δijuiVj does not — that is precisely the equality of the two boxed values.

The Physics

Inner product invariance · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Two arrows lie in one plane, and two frames, S and S′, measure them against axes that differ by a rotation θ. The sim shows what each frame reads for the components, the lengths and the product u·V, so you can sort out which numbers describe the arrows and which describe the axes.

What you'll learn

  • How the components of a vector in a frame depend on the rotation angle θ of the axes.
  • How the length ‖V‖ and the inner product u·V are computed in each frame, and how they depend on θ.
  • How the angle between two arrows is related to u·V.
  • What shifting the origin of the axes does to point coordinates and to vector components.
The same arrows drawn in both panels. Only the axes differ.

What's on screen

  • Frame S (left): fixed grey axes x, y.
  • Frame S′ (right): violet axes x′, y′ turned by θ, with the arc marking θ.
  • Arrow V (blue) and arrow u (amber, stage 4): drawn with dashed projection lines onto each frame's own axes.
  • Readouts under each panel: components, ‖V‖, ‖u‖ and u·V. The sidebar's Invariants panel lists the same three at stage 4.
See itOpen both panels at θ = 30°. Watch for: the same two arrows in both panels, with the S′ axes turned 30° from the S axes.

03

What turning the axes changes

Both panels show the same plane. S′ is S with its axes turned counter-clockwise by θ. Nothing in the plane moves between the panels; only the axes it is measured against do.

  • A frame reads a component by dropping a perpendicular from the arrow's tip onto its own axis. These are the dashed projection lines.
  • Turn the axes and the feet of those lines slide along them. The numbers change, and the arrow does not.
The sim's rule for S′ components from S components, for any arrow A (V or u). The axes turn; the arrow stays put.

With the opening V = (3.00, 4.00), θ = 30° gives (4.60, 1.96) in S′. At θ = 90° it reads (4.00, −3.00): x′ = Vy and y′ = −Vx. At θ = 0° or 360° the two panels agree.

See itCompare V's components in the two panels at θ = 30°. Watch for: Vx, Vy and Vx′, Vy′ are different numbers, while the arrow looks the same in both panels.

Length and inner product agree in both frames

Each frame forms the inner product and the length from its own components, using the Cartesian metric δij (1 when i = j, 0 otherwise):

The lecture figures write |V| for the length ‖V‖ that the sim prints.

The components differ between the panels, yet ‖V‖, ‖u‖ and u·V come out equal in S and S′. This holds at every θ, not only at multiples of 90°.

The sim at its opening settings, θ = 30°, with V = (3, 4) and u = (4, −1).

05

Why the inner product survives the turn

Multiply out the rotated components of any two arrows A and B. The cross terms cancel, and cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 collects the rest.
  • A rotation changes the components, but it leaves δij unchanged. A number built by contracting components with δij therefore cannot depend on θ.
  • Geometrically, u·V = ‖u‖ ‖V‖ cos φ, where φ is the angle between the two arrows. No turn of the axes opens or closes that angle. With the opening arrows, 5.00 × 4.12 × cos 67.2° = 8.00.
  • So for two non-zero arrows, u·V = 0 exactly when they are perpendicular, and both frames agree on it.
See itDrag the tip of u until it is perpendicular to V. Watch for: both u·V boxes read 0.00 while the arrows meet at a right angle in both panels.
06

Moving the origin changes points, not vectors

  • The offset t moves the S′ origin. The S′ coordinates of every point (P, and the tail and tip of V) change, because they are measured from the new origin.
  • A vector is the difference tip − tail, so t cancels. Its components, ‖V‖ and u·V stay as they were.

At stage 3 with θ = 30°, V = tip − tail = (4.5, 3.0) in S and (5.40, 0.35) in S′, whatever t is.

See itSlide the S′ origin from (0, 0) to (2, −1.5) at stage 3. Watch for: the tip's S′ coordinates change, while Vx′, Vy′ and ‖V‖ do not.
07

Where it matters

Lecture 2(d). Alice's axes are Bob's turned by 45°, so her x′ axis lies along the velocity. The lecture notes mark her basis with tildes; this figure and the sim use primes.
  • Speed. Bob and Alice track one particle with axes 45° apart. Their velocity components differ, but ‖V‖² = v² for both, so they agree on the speed.
  • Distance. The separation of P = (0, 0) and Q = (1, 1) in Bob's axes becomes (√2, 0) in Alice's. Both get √2.
  • The next step in the course. Keep the recipe but change the metric, with a relative minus sign between the time and space terms. The number that stays fixed is then the spacetime interval.
Go deeper: the matrix form of the cancellation
  • Write the S′ components as R times the S components, with R = (cos θ, sin θ; −sin θ, cos θ). Then u′·V′ = (Ru)ᵀ(RV) = uᵀ(RᵀR)V.
  • Because RᵀR = 1 for a rotation, u′·V′ = uᵀV. That is the cancellation of the previous section in one line.
08

Summary

In one line. Turning the axes changes an arrow's components. The length ‖V‖ and the inner product u·V, built with the Cartesian metric δij, take the same value in every frame.

Key points

  • S′ components come from S components by the rotation R(θ). The arrows are never moved.
  • u·V = δijuiVj and ‖V‖ = √(V·V) agree in S and S′, because R leaves δij unchanged.
  • u·V = ‖u‖ ‖V‖ cos φ, so u·V = 0 means the arrows are perpendicular in every frame.

Common mix-ups

  • "Turning the axes changes ‖V‖ or u·V." It changes the components only. Both panels agree at every θ.
  • "u·V = 0 means perpendicular in S only." Both frames report 0, so the arrows are perpendicular in both.
  • "Sliding the S′ origin changes V's components." It changes point coordinates. V is a difference of two points, and the shift cancels.

Things to try on your own

  • At stage 4, set θ to 90° and check the S′ rows against x′ = Vy, y′ = −Vx and the same rule for u.
  • Drag the tip of u to about (5, −1.25), a quarter longer. Predict the new u·V, then read both boxes.
  • At stage 3, set t = (2.0, −1.5) with the sliders and compare the tail and tip in S′ with their values at t = (0, 0).
